The '''university''' as an institution took shape in medieval [[Higher education|Latin Europe]].
A medieval university was a corporation organised during the Middle Ages for the
purpose of higher education.<ref name="wp-med" /> Historians usually reserve the
term for an institution that medieval sources called a ''studium generale''.<ref name="wp-list" />

== The studium generale ==

The ''studium generale'' was a new entity for advanced study that appeared in
Europe from the 12th century, arising out of gatherings of masters and scholars
in early centres of learning such as Bologna, Paris and Oxford.<ref name="stanford" />
The term ''studium generale'' itself came into customary use at the start of the
13th century and denoted a place that welcomed students from everywhere, not
only from the local district.<ref name="wp-sg" />

== From guild to institution ==

The Latin ''universitas'' originally named a guild or voluntary association of
individual masters, rather than a single institution run by an organised staff;
only later did the word come to mean a university in the modern sense.<ref name="hoi" />

== Charters ==

The first university charters were issued in 13th-century Europe. The ''studium
generale'' created by a charter of Emperor Frederick II in 1224 is widely
regarded as the first deliberately founded university.<ref name="wp-charter" />
